description:
We are a team of Computer Science students passionate about space, space exploration and the future of human life beyond Earth.

Therefore the challenge we are taking: we aim to develop an interactive Martian Map to help future astronauts explore Mars more safely and efficiently through accessible scientific data and navigation tools.

We are excited to collaborate, learn and turn our project into something meaningful!
summary:
Astronaut Route Exploration System is an interactive map for planning and evaluating routes between two points in a specific region of Mars. It considers factors such as temperature, radiation, and terrain slope to help users choose routes that prioritize crew and equipment safety or reduce travel time.

Our project addresses the challenge “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map.” As space exploration advances, crewed missions beyond the Moon—and especially missions to Mars—are becoming increasingly realistic. However, the Red Planet’s harsh environment poses serious risks to astronauts and the equipment they rely on, including rovers and other exploration vehicles.

The system helps future missions navigate these conditions. By highlighting areas with extreme temperatures, high radiation, or difficult terrain, it allows users to avoid hazardous zones and compare possible routes. Each mission can adapt its itinerary to its priorities: choosing a safer path to protect the crew and equipment, or a faster one when saving time is more important.

Our goal is to support future expeditions with a clear tool for making route decisions on the Martian surface. This can help crews reach locations of scientific interest efficiently while accounting for the challenges of travelling across Mars.
details:
ARES is an interactive route planner for the first crews to drive on Mars. You pick a start and a destination on the real terrain of Jezero Crater, where NASA’s Perseverance rover landed in 2021. ARES then tells you where you can drive, how long it will take, how much energy it will cost and what risks you will face on the way. It all runs in the browser, built entirely on open NASA and USGS data.

How it works

  1. Explore Mars from orbit. A 2D map lets you switch between orbital datasets:
    • MOLA laser altimetry as the base;
    • CTX imagery at 6 m per pixel and HiRISE down to 25 cm, where boulders a meter across are visible;
    • elevation and slope from the USGS 20 m digital terrain model;
    • night-time cold from THEMIS infrared;
    • a radiation estimate.
    • Fastest: minimizes driving time.
    • Safest: avoids slopes and rough ground, even if the route is longer.
    • Least energy: accounts for rolling resistance and hauling 3,000 kg uphill.
    • simulated rocker-bogie suspension, with dust, wheel tracks and rocks;
    • a chase view and the Navcam view from the mast;
    • a minimap;
    • a Sun computed for Jezero’s latitude, so sunsets turn blue as they really do on Mars.
  2. Get a GO / NO-GO. A mission report combines travel time, remaining range, battery, slopes, night cold and accumulated radiation dose, measured against NASA’s 600 mSv career limit. It returns a clear verdict, GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, with the reasons behind it.

How we compute the science

  • Slope: the gradient of the 20 m terrain model at a scale of about 60 m. The thresholds are 8°, 15° and an 18° vehicle limit, and they are the same across the whole app.
  • Time and energy: based on a pressurized rover similar to NASA’s SEV concept. We assumed the figures: 8 km/h on flat ground, 72 h autonomy, a 60 kWh battery and 3,000 kg. Speed drops with slope and roughness, and energy includes the climbing work.
  • Radiation: starts from the 0.64 mSv per day measured on the surface by the RAD instrument on Curiosity. It is reduced where the terrain blocks part of the sky (the horizon is computed in 16 directions out to 3 km) and adjusted for altitude.
  • Night cold: taken from THEMIS night-time infrared. We show it as relative (“colder than X% of the area”) rather than inventing temperatures nobody has measured.

Benefits and intended impact

  • For mission planners: a fast way to compare routes and understand their risks before anyone leaves the habitat.
  • For crews: one clear answer, “can we go, and what will it cost us?”, instead of a stack of separate datasets.
  • For education and outreach: anyone can plan a traverse on real Martian terrain and see the trade-offs between speed, safety and energy.
  • Reusable: the pipeline works with any site that has a terrain model and orbital imagery.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, with no backend and nothing to install; it runs in any modern browser on an ordinary laptop.
  • Libraries: Leaflet for the 2D map, Three.js and WebGL for 3D, and Web Workers to run the route searches in parallel.
    • USGS Astrogeology CTX 20 m DTM (Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation);
    • MOLA MEGDR;
    • MRO CTX and HiRISE mosaics through NASA Mars Trek;
    • THEMIS night-time infrared;
    • Curiosity RAD measurements;
    • NASA’s Perseverance 3D model.
  • Development: Git and GitHub, with AI-assisted development (Claude Code).

What makes it creative

ARES turns planetary datasets that normally live in scientific tools into something anyone understands in seconds: click two points, compare three routes, then ride behind the rover. A presentation mode built into the app tells the whole story on its own.

Factors we considered

  • Crew safety first: slope limits, radiation dose and night cold are part of every route, not extras.
  • Scientific honesty: we label what is measured, what is modeled and what is assumed.
  • Performance: typed arrays, multithreading and preloading keep it smooth in a normal browser.
  • Clarity for non-experts: the same color thresholds everywhere, plain-language verdicts, and an English interface.
